messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] 3-level spatial autocorrelation model in BUGS
parts:
Dear Courtney,

offlist I send you code for a 4-level nested ANOVA according to Gelman (2006) and the Ecology paper by Qian and Shen (2007). You can see there how they code this. I am not sure about the plot effects in your code. I think I would also treat them as random effects in the analysis.

The other thing I was wondering about is why you don't use the density estimates with their SEs directly in a Normal mixed model ? From what I understand you do a two-step hierarchical model, with the distance sampling analysis coming first and then in the second step, you do stats on stats. So to propagate the uncertainty in the plot density estimates you could use both the density point estimates and their uncertainty (SE) as shown (with code given) in the JAPPL paper by McCarthy & Masters. Link and Sauer (Ecology, 2002, hierarchical model for trends of many species) have also done the same thing.

Re. testing for plot or transect effects, I think the DIC could work -- From what I understand, you should not believe the DIC for mixture models (e.g., Nmix or site-occ), but when all your random effects are continuous, that's probably OK.

Kind regards  --  Marc

From: unma...@googlegroups.com [unma...@googlegroups.com] on behalf of CAmundson [amun...@umn.edu]
Sent: 18 December 2012 20:25
To: unma...@googlegroups.com
Subject: [unmarked] 3-level spatial autocorrelation model in BUGS

Hi All-
 
Forgive me as this doesn't directly pertain to unmarked, but I'm using unmarked output...and the data are similar...so I thought I'd see if anyone would be able to help. 
 
I ran analyses in unmarked to estimate density for a series of avian point counts.  I would like to run a few species in BUGS to examine spatial autocorrelation - and whether or not it was important.  I'm guessing not, but editors aren't interested in my opinion, go figure.  I'm NOT using 'car' models, but rather blocking the analysis based on nested group variables...  Surveys were conducted at points (surveyed once), every 500 m along point-transects that were randomly selected within larger 10 km x 10 km plots (i.e., site in transect in plot).  I would like to include nested random effects for transects and plots.  I think I got the transect effect model working just fine - what I'm having trouble with is coding how to nest transects within plots.  Really, I'm only interested in an overall effect of transect and plot, but this output provides estimates for each transect and plot - which I think of as adjustments to the intercept for each group?  
 
Bah!  With help from a friend, this model works and produces beta coefficients similar to the unmarked analysis.  However, a) I'm not entirely sure the nesting structure is what I want and b) I have no idea how to interpret whether or not the transect-plot effect is important?  Overlapping CIs for each transect-plot?  DIC is lower for this model compared to the transect only and no spatial correlation model, but Bayesian p-values are hovering around 0.88, which doesn't make me feel fabulous about it.  Here's what I have...the part that's troubling me is in bold...snippets of code were taken from both Kery-Schaub books, Gelman and Hill, Royle and Dorazio and Patuxent workshop materials.
 
Thanks so much!  C-
 
logD = log of the predicted detection probability at each site (unmarked output using predict function and distsamp) - here used as an offset
nPlot = # plots = 63
nTran = # transects = 169
nsites = # sites = 1021
10 betas for habitat effects
alpha.tran = transect effect - nested within plot
p.plot = plot effect

# now with spatial autocorrelation for transect and plot ###############################################
sink("gcspautotranplot.txt")
cat("
    model {
    # Priors for fixed effects
    alpha ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta2 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta3 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta4 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta5 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta6 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta7 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta8 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta9 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta10 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
 
#Prior distributions for random effect of plot
        for (p in 1:nPlot){
        p.plot[p] ~ dunif(0,10)   # creating a separate mean and sd for each plot
        sd.plot[p] ~ dunif(0,10)
        tau.plot[p] <- pow(sd.plot[p],-2)
       
     }
# prior distributions for transects nested within plot
for(t in 1:nTran){
    alpha.tran[t] ~ dnorm(p.plot[plot[t]], tau.plot[plot[t]])  # so the 'random effect' for transects from the same plot are more similar
}
# now when t=2 it will be referencing transect 2 and since the plot.index vector is the same length as the number of transects it will pull
# a value for 'plot' associated with the second transect, this 'plot' value (which would be '1' in the example) will index the first p.plot and # first tau.plot distribution generated
 
    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:nsites) {
    C[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    log(lambda[i])<- 1*logD[i] +alpha+ beta1*tshrub[i] + beta2*herbmes[i] + beta3*elmean[i] +
    beta4*elmean[i]*elmean[i] + beta5*mixed[i] + beta6*dec[i] + beta7*dlichen[i]+ beta8*dshrub[i]
    + beta9*spruce[i] + beta10*sitka_wh[i]+ alpha.tran[transect[i]]
    }
    
    #goodness of fit
   
    for (i in 1:nsites){
    residual[i]<-C[i]-lambda[i]# residuals for observed data
    predicted[i]<-lambda[i]
    sq[i]<-pow(residual[i],2)
   
    # generate replicate data
    C.new[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
    sq.new[i]<-pow(C.new[i]-predicted[i],2) # squared residuals for new data
    }
   
    # Derived parameters
    fit<-sum(sq[])
    fit.new<-sum(sq.new[])
    test<-step(fit.new-fit)
    bayesp<-mean(test)
    totalL<-sum(lambda[])  # equal to sum(count) despite offset...
}
    ", fill=TRUE)
sink()
# Bundle data
win.data<-list(C=gcspoffset$count, tshrub = gcspoffset$tshrub,herbmes = gcspoffset$herbmes,
               elmean = gcspoffset$elmean, mixed = gcspoffset$mixed, dec=gcspoffset$dec, dlichen=
                 gcspoffset$dlichen, dshrub=gcspoffset$dshrub, spruce=gcspoffset$spruce, sitka_wh=
                 gcspoffset$sitka_wh, transect=gcspoffset$tranid, plot=gcspoffset$plotid,
               nTran=length(unique(gcspoffset$tranid)), nPlot=length(unique(gcspoffset$plotid)),
               logD = log(gcspoffset$det), nsites=length(gcspoffset$tshrub))
# Inits function
inits<- function() { list(alpha=0.3,beta1=0.15,beta2=0.15,beta3=-0.15,beta4=-0.29,beta5=-0.5,
                          beta6=0.13,beta7=-0.2,beta8=-0.2,beta9=-0.17,beta10=-0.21,
                          sd.plot=runif(63),
                         p.plot=runif(63), alpha.tran=runif(169)) }

# parameters to estimate
params<-c("alpha", "beta1", "beta2","beta3","beta4","beta5","beta6","beta7","beta8","beta9",
          "beta10", "sd.plot","p.plot","alpha","totalL","fit","fit.new","bayesp","alpha.tran")

messages.subject: Re: 3-level spatial autocorrelation model in BUGS
parts:
Thanks Marc - I realized I have no good excuse for not formatting it as a mixture model other than I've been too preoccupied with getting the random effects working!  Your code helped me realize I had a couple things incorrect.
 
1.  overall alpha should be in the top level (plot)
2.  tau for transect should be it's own variable (and not  tau.plot)
 
I quickly recreated the code with simulated data for illustration.  If anyone has comments, questions, or finds additional errors let me know.  Thanks!
 
# Simulated bird data
# 1000 point counts
# points were spaced at 500m intervals along point-transects - ~ 5 points per transect
# transects were randomly selected within larger 10km x 10km plots in an area
# looking for potential spatial correlation in counts at the transect and plot level
# Here the simulated data are just to show you the format - they're not explicitly spatially correlated
 
set.seed(4321)
# LEVEL 1
# sites
nsites<- 1000
# site level covariate
habitat<-rnorm(nsites) # a covariate value
# relationship between habitat and count
lambda<- exp(0.3 + .5*habitat)
C<-rpois(nsites,lambda) # site-specific counts
# LEVEL 2
# transects
ntran<-169
# transect id for each site
transect<-as.integer(seq(1,169,length.out=1000))
transect[1:3]<-169 # transect 169 only had one site associated with it - giving it a few more
# there is probably a much better way to do this
# LEVEL 3
# plots
nplot<-63
# plot id for each site
plot<-as.integer(seq(1,63,length.out=1000))
plot[1:5]<-63  # same issue as tran
# Detection probability from a different analysis (I didn't estimate detection in BUGS because I'm still having
# trouble working covariates into Andy's distance sampling code)
pcap<-runif(1000,min=0.2,max=0.6) # make between 0.2 - 0.6

# now with BUGS spatial autocorrelation for transect and plot ###############################################
sink("auto.txt")
cat("
    model {
   
    # LEVEL 3
#Prior distributions for random effect of plot

for (p in 1:nplot){  # loop over all plots
    alpha.plot[p] ~ dnorm(alpha.over,tau.plot)   # plot effect -  contains overall alpha
    }       
    # Fixed level 3 priors
    sd.plot ~ dunif(0,10)
    tau.plot <- pow(sd.plot,-2)
    alpha.over ~ dnorm(0,0.001)  # fixed overall intercept
   
    # LEVEL 2
# prior distributions for transects nested within plot

for(t in 1:ntran){  # loop over all transects
    alpha.tran[t] ~ dnorm(alpha.plot[plot[t]], tau.tran) # here mean of transect effect is related to plot - so nesting
    # the effect of transect within plot - but assigned it's own tau
    }
    # fixed level 2 priors
    sd.tran ~ dunif(0,10)
    tau.tran <- pow(sd.tran,-2)
   
    # LEVEL 1
    # fixed level 1 prior
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)  # site level habitat covariate
   
    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:nsites) {  # loop over all sites
    C[i] ~ dbin(pcap[i],N[i])  # mixture model - C is count per site
    N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])  # N is abundance - latent here
    log(lambda[i])<- alpha.tran[transect[i]] + beta1*habitat[i] # for likelihood - intercept is based on random
    # effects
   
    }
   
    }
    ", fill=TRUE)
sink()
# Bundle data
win.data<-list(C=C, habitat=habitat, transect=transect, plot=plot,
               ntran=ntran, nplot=nplot,pcap=pcap,nsites= nsites)
# Inits function  VERY SENSITIVE TO INITS FOR N - make close to count and avoid zeros
inits<- function() { list(alpha.over=2,beta1=0.5,
                          sd.plot=runif(1),sd.tran=runif(1),alpha.over=runif(1),
                          alpha.plot=runif(63), alpha.tran=runif(169),N=C+1) }
# parameters to estimate
params<-c("alpha.over", "beta1",
          "alpha.plot", "sd.tran",
          "sd.plot","alpha.tran","totalN")
# MCMC settings
nc<-3

On Wednesday, December 19, 2012 10:33:25 AM UTC-9, CAmundson wrote:
 
 Thanks Marc - I realized I have no good excuse for not formatting it as a mixture model other than I've been too preoccupied with getting the random effects working!  Your code helped me realize I had a couple things incorrect.
 
1.  overall alpha should be in the top level (plot)
2.  tau for transect should be it's own variable (and not  tau.plot)
 
I quickly recreated the code with simulated data for illustration.  If anyone has comments, questions, or finds additional errors let me know.  Thanks!
 
# Simulated bird data
# 1000 point counts
# points were spaced at 500m intervals along point-transects - ~ 5 points per transect
# transects were randomly selected within larger 10km x 10km plots in an area
# looking for potential spatial correlation in counts at the transect and plot level
# Here the simulated data are just to show you the format - they're not explicitly spatially correlated
 
set.seed(4321)
# LEVEL 1
# sites
nsites<- 1000
# site level covariate
habitat<-rnorm(nsites) # a covariate value
# relationship between habitat and count
lambda<- exp(0.3 + .5*habitat)
C<-rpois(nsites,lambda) # site-specific counts
# LEVEL 2
# transects
ntran<-169
# transect id for each site
transect<-as.integer(seq(1,169,length.out=1000))
transect[1:3]<-169 # transect 169 only had one site associated with it - giving it a few more
# there is probably a much better way to do this
# LEVEL 3
# plots
nplot<-63
# plot id for each site
plot<-as.integer(seq(1,63,length.out=1000))
plot[1:5]<-63  # same issue as tran
# Detection probability from a different analysis (I didn't estimate detection in BUGS because I'm still having
# trouble working covariates into Andy's distance sampling code)
pcap<-runif(1000,min=0.2,max=0.6) # make between 0.2 - 0.6

# now with BUGS spatial autocorrelation for transect and plot ###############################################
sink("auto.txt")
cat("
    model {
   
    # LEVEL 3
    #Prior distributions for random effect of plot
    for (p in 1:nplot){  # loop over all plots
    alpha.plot[p] ~ dnorm(alpha.over,tau.plot)   # plot effect -  contains overall alpha
    }       
    # Fixed level 3 priors
    sd.plot ~ dunif(0,10)
    tau.plot <- pow(sd.plot,-2)
    alpha.over ~ dnorm(0,0.001)  # fixed overall intercept
   
    # LEVEL 2   
    # prior distributions for transects nested within plot
    for(t in 1:ntran){  # loop over all transects
    alpha.tran[t] ~ dnorm(alpha.plot[plot[t]], tau.tran) # here mean of transect effect is related to plot - so nesting
    # the effect of transect within plot - but assigned it's own tau
    }
    # fixed level 2 priors
    sd.tran ~ dunif(0,10)
    tau.tran <- pow(sd.tran,-2)
   
    # LEVEL 1
    # fixed level 1 prior
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)  # site level habitat covariate
   
    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:nsites) {  # loop over all sites
    C[i] ~ dbin(pcap[i],N[i])  # mixture model - C is count per site
    N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])  # N is abundance - latent here
    log(lambda[i])<- alpha.tran[transect[i]] + beta1*habitat[i] # for likelihood - intercept is based on random
    # effects

}
    # DERIVED PARAMETERS
   totalN<-sum(N[])  # abundance across all sites

}
    ", fill=TRUE)
sink()
# Bundle data
win.data<-list(C=C, habitat=habitat, transect=transect, plot=plot,
               ntran=ntran, nplot=nplot,pcap=pcap,nsites= nsites)
# Inits function  VERY SENSITIVE TO INITS FOR N - make close to count and avoid zeros
inits<- function() { list(alpha.over=2,beta1=0.5,
                          sd.plot=runif(1),sd.tran=runif(1),alpha.over=runif(1),
                          alpha.plot=runif(63), alpha.tran=runif(169),N=C+1) }
# parameters to estimate
params<-c("alpha.over", "beta1",
          "alpha.plot", "sd.tran",
          "sd.plot","alpha.tran","totalN")
# MCMC settings
nc<-3
ni<-500
nb<-10
nt<-2
#Start Gibbs Sampler
system.time(outw<-bugs(data=win.data, inits=inits, parameters.to.save=params,
                       model.file="auto.txt",n.thin=nt, n.chains=nc, n.burnin=nb, n.iter=ni,
                       debug=TRUE,bugs.directory="C:/WinBUGS/WinBUGS14/"))

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Re: 3-level spatial autocorrelation model in BUGS
parts:
Looks good to me except that I think you need a plot effect as well in the line with the linear predictor. I would change the line to something like:

log(lambda[i])<- alpha.tran[transect[i]] + alpha.plot[plot[i]] + beta1*habitat[i] # for likelihood - intercept is based on random

BTW, the way you had it, this would be centered on zero, because the overall mean is in the prior for the plot effects.

And you could also add a random point effect, to account for overdispersion relative to the Poisson. But perhaps that might be too much ?

Regards  --  Marc

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: 3-level spatial autocorrelation model in BUGS
parts:
Courtney,

Have you seen Chelgren et al. (2011) Herpetological Conservation and Biology?  They have WinBUGS code for distance sampling that seems to work well.  They calculate the likelihood of sigma in a half-normal model based on the individual distances, and then use that sigma to compute a capture probability for individuals within the effective area of sampling.  That capture probability would then obviously be "pcap" in your model, but otherwise your general model structure would be unchanged.

-Dan
